read.sections.0.text.note: Borobudur's terraces = ลานชั้น (not นาขั้นบันได, which is AAS10's farming terrace); galleries = ระเบียง; openwork stupa = สถูปโปร่ง; relics = พระธาตุ.
read.sections.0.text.source:
Buildings guide how people move. An entrance invites people to come from one direction. A passage can slow them down, and stairs change their level and their view. These choices matter in sacred buildings. There, moving through a place can be part of religious practice, not just a way to reach the end.

Borobudur, in the Kedu Valley of Central Java, was built in the eighth and ninth centuries. UNESCO describes square terraces rising to round platforms, with a large stupa on top. A stupa is a Buddhist sacred monument, often linked with relics (the remains of a holy person) or with remembering. Galleries, or long walkways, hold carved reliefs. A relief is a sculpture that stands out from a flat background. Smaller openwork stupas, with gaps in their stone, stand above. The photographs show the upper part of this layout. They are not views of every gallery or of the whole ground plan.
read.sections.0.text.back:
Buildings shape how people move. An entrance invites people in from one direction, a passage can slow people down, and stairs change their level and view. These choices matter in sacred buildings, because there moving through a place can be part of religious practice, not just a way to reach the end.

Borobudur, in the Kedu valley of Central Java, was built in the 8th and 9th centuries. UNESCO describes square terraces rising to round terraces, with a large stupa at the top. A stupa is a Buddhist sacred structure, often connected with relics (remains of a holy person) or remembrance. Long galleries or walkways have reliefs. A relief is a carving that rises from a flat surface. Smaller open-work stupas with gaps in the stone stand at the top. The photograph shows the upper part of this layout, not every gallery level or the whole plan.

read.sections.1.text.note: Candi Sewu = จันดีเซวู (Thai also writes จันทิเสวู); Hindu temples = เทวาลัยฮินดู; images = รูปเคารพ. The Met as พิพิธภัณฑ์ศิลปะเมโทรโพลิแทน. Reviewer: spelling of The Met made the same as AAS01–AAS05 (เมโทรโพลิทัน, not เมโทรโพลิแทน).
read.sections.1.text.source:
Buddhism grew from the teachings of the Buddha and spread through many societies. Its art and buildings took different forms in different places. The Metropolitan Museum of Art explains how stupas became places of devotion and pilgrimage. A pilgrimage is a journey to a place of religious importance. Stupas had paths for moving around them. Their meaning comes from religious traditions and practices. Their shape alone does not explain everything a visitor might believe or do.

In eighth- and ninth-century Java, contact with India helped texts and images travel. Javanese patrons and makers adapted these ideas, using local images and building knowledge. The Smithsonian places Borobudur alongside other Buddhist monuments on the island, including Candi Sewu. Central Java also had major Hindu temples. So Buddhism was important within a varied religious landscape. Calling Borobudur "Indonesian" places it in the present. Its builders lived under earlier Javanese rulers, before the modern nation existed.
read.sections.1.text.back:
Buddhism grew from the Buddha's teachings and spread to many societies. Buddhist art and buildings took different forms in each place. The Metropolitan Museum of Art explains how stupas became places for worship and pilgrimage. Pilgrimage is a journey to a religiously important place. Stupas have paths for walking around. A stupa's meaning comes from tradition and religious practice; form alone doesn't explain everything visitors might believe or do.

In Java in the 8th and 9th centuries, contact with India helped texts and sacred images arrive. Javanese patrons and craftsmen adapted these ideas, using local visual styles and building knowledge. The Smithsonian groups Borobudur with other Buddhist monuments on the island, including Candi Sewu. Central Java also has large Hindu temples, so Buddhism was important among a varied religious landscape. Calling Borobudur “Indonesian” is a view from today: its builders lived under earlier Javanese rulers, before the modern country existed.

read.sections.1.simpler.source:
Buddhism began with the teachings of the Buddha. It spread to many places. Its art and buildings look different in each place. A museum in New York says stupas became places for prayer and pilgrimage. A pilgrimage is a journey to a holy place. People walked around stupas on paths. Their meaning comes from religious practice. Their shape alone does not tell us what people believe.

At this time, Java had contact with India. Texts and pictures came from there. People in Java changed these ideas. They used their own pictures and building skills. Java had other Buddhist temples too, such as Candi Sewu. It also had big Hindu temples. Today Borobudur is in Indonesia. But its builders lived under kings of Java, long before Indonesia existed.
read.sections.1.simpler.back:
Buddhism began with the Buddha's teachings, then spread to many places. Buddhist art and buildings look different in each place. A museum in New York says stupas became places for prayer and pilgrimage. Pilgrimage is a journey to a sacred place. People walk around a stupa on a path. A stupa's meaning comes from religious practice. Form alone doesn't tell what people believe.

At that time, Java had contact with India. Texts and images came from there. People in Java adapted these ideas, using their own images and building skills. Java also has other Buddhist temples, such as Candi Sewu, and also large Hindu temples. Today Borobudur is in Indonesia, but its builders lived under Javanese kings, long before there was a country called Indonesia.

read.sections.2.heading.source: A journey, its makers and later changes

read.sections.2.text.note: Worshippers = ผู้มาสักการะ. Robert E. Gordon kept in Latin (a person's name).
read.sections.2.text.source:
Art historian Robert E. Gordon connects Borobudur's paths, changing levels, sculpture and images with a Buddhist journey towards understanding. Worshippers could walk around the galleries, passing carved stories, then climb towards the upper terraces. Body, image, space and religious meaning worked together. A relief is more than a picture added after a building is finished. Where it is placed can shape how people experience the monument.

The monument was also a social project. Its royal supporters are linked with Java's Śailendra dynasty, a ruling family, around 800 CE. A patron is a person or group who supports the making of an artwork or building. Building and carving stone on this scale needed organised resources and many kinds of skilled work. Naming the patrons should not make the builders disappear, even when surviving records tell us more about rulers than about workers. Religious ideas travelled, but the people who made this place made practical and artistic choices.

Borobudur has changed over time. UNESCO helped with major restoration in the 1970s. A photograph today records how the stone looks now, not an untouched scene from the ninth century. We can study the site with respect, without assuming that every Buddhist community, building or visitor has the same experience.
read.sections.2.text.back:
Robert E. Gordon, an art historian, connects Borobudur's paths, changing levels, sculpture and images with a journey towards understanding in the Buddhist way. Worshippers could walk around the galleries, past carved stories, then climb up to the upper terraces. Body, image, space and religious meaning work together. So the reliefs are more than pictures added after the building was finished; where they are placed can shape people's experience of the monument.

This monument was also the work of a society. Royal patrons were connected with Java's Śailendra dynasty, a ruling family, around 800 CE. A patron is a person or group who supports making art or buildings. Building and carving stone at this scale needed systematically organised resources and many kinds of craft. Naming patrons shouldn't make the builders disappear, even though surviving records tell more about rulers than about workers. Religious ideas travelled from elsewhere, but the people who built this place made both practical and artistic decisions.

Borobudur changed over time. UNESCO helped with a major restoration in the 1970s. A photograph today records how the stones look now, not an image untouched since the 9th century. We can study this place with respect without assuming that all Buddhist communities, buildings or visitors have the same experience.

read.sections.2.simpler.source:
One art historian links the paths, levels and carvings to a Buddhist journey. It is a journey towards understanding. People walked around the walkways and passed carved stories. Then they climbed to the top. Body, pictures and space worked together. So a relief is not just a picture on a wall. Where it is placed changes how people move and see.

The monument was supported by kings of the Śailendra family, around 800 CE. A patron is a person who pays for or supports a building. But many skilled workers built and carved it. Old records tell us more about kings than workers. We should still remember the workers. Ideas came from far away. But the people who built it made their own choices.

Borobudur has changed. In the 1970s, UNESCO helped repair it. So a photo today shows how it looks now. It does not show it as it was long ago. Not every Buddhist group, building or visitor is the same.
read.sections.2.simpler.back:
An art historian connects the paths, levels and carvings with a journey in the Buddhist way, a journey towards understanding. People walk around the walkways and past carved stories, then climb up to the top. Body, image and space work together. So the reliefs are not just pictures on a wall. Where they are placed changes how people walk and see.

Kings of the Śailendra dynasty were the patrons of this monument, around 800 CE. A patron is someone who pays for or supports making a building. But many craftsmen built and carved it. Old records tell more about kings than about workers. We should still remember the workers. The ideas came from far away, but the builders made their own decisions.

Borobudur has changed. In the 1970s UNESCO helped repair it. So a photograph today shows how it is now, not how it was long ago. Buddhist groups, buildings and visitors are not all the same everywhere.

sensitiveNotes.0.source: Borobudur is a sacred place that people still use for worship. Teach Buddhist belief and practice as a tradition people hold, not as something learners must agree with. No learner is asked to share their religion or take part in any practice; a learner can explain the documented meaning of the path without accepting it personally.
sensitiveNotes.0.back: Borobudur is a sacred place people still use for worship. Teach Buddhist beliefs and practices as traditions people hold, not something learners must agree with. No learner is asked to tell about their religion or take part in any practice. Learners can explain the recorded meaning of the path without personally accepting it.

educatorNotes.0.note: Added the Thai word การเดินประทักษิณ for circumambulation, since a Thai teacher would introduce the Thai word.
educatorNotes.0.source: Borobudur is not a general example that explains every Buddhist building or all Buddhist beliefs. Keep noticing a physical feature apart from explaining its religious significance, and keep the ninth-century Javanese setting apart from present-day Indonesia. The brief's vocabulary also gives circumambulation (moving around a sacred object or place); it is left out of the key words to keep the reading plain, and the reading explains the idea as walking around a stupa. Introduce the word if it helps your group.
educatorNotes.0.back: Borobudur is not a general example explaining every Buddhist building or all Buddhist belief. Separate observing physical features from explaining religious significance, and separate 9th-century Java from present-day Indonesia. The lesson's specification also lists circumambulation (pradakshina, walking around a sacred object or place), but it is not among the key words, to keep the reading easy; the reading explains the idea as walking around the stupa. Introduce the word if it helps your group.

educatorNotes.2.source: UNESCO's Borobudur page supports the place, the broad dates, the terraces and stupas, the reliefs and the 1970s restoration. Robert E. Vidya Dehejia's Met essay (2007) is used only for the religious setting of stupas.
educatorNotes.2.back: UNESCO's Borobudur page supports the place, broad dates, terraces and stupas, reliefs and the 1970s restoration. Robert E. Gordon's Smarthistory essay gives the interpretation of the path; avoid its “rediscovery” framing and its precise construction claims, and don't use the essay's photographs. educatorNotes.3.source: The Smithsonian label for a Head of the Buddha (F1978.35) supports Javanese adaptation of images and building knowledge within wider contact with India; that object's original temple is uncertain. UNESCO's Prambanan page is used only to show that Central Java also had major Hindu temples; its dates disagree with each other, so no date is given for them.
